speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING
subsubtopic: CONVERSATIONS WITH PRESIDENT ROOSEVELT
speechtext:
Before the orders of the day are
proceeded with, it is perhaps desirable that I should make a short statement. The President of the United States invited the dominion to send a representative to the conference which is being held at Washington with many of the nations of the world. I arrived in Washington on Monday and I left on Saturday. Before leaving, the following joint statement was agreed upon between the president and myself and given to the press:
Our conversations have been eminently satisfactory in establishing a common ground of approach to the principal problems of the world monetary and economic conference. We are agreed that our primary need is to ensure an increase in the general level of commodity prices. To this end simultaneous action must be taken both in the economic and in the monetary fields. Economic and monetary policies must be adjusted to permit a freer international exchange of commodities.
It is recognized that as soon as practicable an international monetary standard must be restored, with arrangements which will ensure
a more satisfactory operation of monetary relationships. We have examined a series of proposals for the more effective employment of silver.
No one of these problems can be profitably dealt with in isolation from the others, nor can any single country accomplish a satisfactory solution.	We therefore recognize the vital
importance to mankind of the world economic conference and the necessity of reaching, in the weeks which remain before it is convened, as great a measure of mutual understanding as possible.
We have also discussed the problems peculiar to the United States and Canada. We have agreed to begin a search for means to increase the exchange of commodities between our two countries, and thereby promote not only economic betterment on the North American continent, but also the general improvement of world conditions.
I can only say further that on behalf of this dominion I thanked the President of the United States with great sincerity for his courtesy and kindness extended to the Canadian representative. I might read to this chamber the words that I uttered over the radio on Saturday at a quarter to three as I was leaving Washington:
I have come to speak a few words of farewell this afternoon before I return to Canada. We Canadians do not feel that we are strangers in your hospitable country, nor I hope do the people of the United States feel themselves to be _ strangers when they come as welcome visitors to Canada. We are friendly neighbours and speak to one another as such. This is natural and proper. But I am nevertheless deeply impressed with the warm welcome and generous hospitality which I have received from your president, your secretary of state and his assistants, and from all those with whom I have come in contact. I will carry with me many pleasant memories which I shall long cherish.
I concluded my observations as to the future attitude of this dominion with respect to the matters under consideration with these words:
Acknowledging your president's wide vision and unselfish purpose, his steady courage and sincerity, his rare patience and determination, I promise that Canada will play its part in the task of seeking world recovery through cooperation with the United States and all the other nations of the world.

speechtext: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 27, to amend the Bank Act.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF CHARTERS FOR ONE YEAR-POSTPONEMENT OF REVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to postpone for a year the obligation which is placed upon parliament by statute to revise the Bank Act once in every ten years. There must be very strong reasons for taking a course such as this.
At this stage of the session I am not going to take exception to postponement of the revision of the Bank Act until next session, but I wish to take very strong exception to the government having decided at the outset to postpone the revision for another year. I do not think that the reasons given by the administration in the speech from the throne and by the Prime Minister at the time of the debate on the address, are sufficient to justify the action which the government decided at the outset to take of postponing the revision for another year. There are no more important questions at the present time facing this country in common with other countries than those arising out of matters pertaining to banking, credit and currency. It is a misfortune that members of this parliament have not had opportunity, in the banking committee, to discuss these questions very fully and to make at this present session, if thought advisable as a result of the discussion, the amendments that should be made to the Bank Act at this time. I am inclined to think that the government's action was merely a failure to grapple concretely and immediately with this most urgent and pressing of our problems.

Bank Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
I know the reason given has been that there is to be a world monetary and economic conference which will have to consider these matters. May I point out to my hon. friends opposite that while the same conference is going to be equally concerned with currency and credit problems of other countries, the fact that the conference was in contemplation did not in anyway prevent the United States congress, even immediately following a general election, with many very pressing problems before it, from taking immediate action with respect to certain features of its banking legislation. If it were possible for that country in so short a time to meet to consider what was necessary in the way of revision of its banking laws, there was equally strong reason why we in Canada should have taken a similar course especially where the obligation was imposed upon us by statute.
May I say also that I think the government was under a misaprehension as to what had taken place with respect to previous revisions. Speaking on the address in reply to the speech from the throne the Prime Minister stated that there had been several postponements of the revision of the Bank Act, and that on the last occasion there had been two if not three such postponements. I do not think in making that statement that my right hon. friend, speaking from memory, had any intention of in any way misrepresenting the situation, but certainly he was quite wide of the mark in what he said. I should like to read the remarks of the Prime Minister, which appear in Hansard for October 10, 1932:
. . . several times in the past bank charters have been renewed for a year only. When was the last revision? After the war they were extended because the chaotic conditions had not yet righted themselves and in the light of the additional knowledge obtained and secured by reason of what was going on in the world at the time it was believed that our domestic problems would be best dealt with by such an extension. The present Bank Act was not passed when the previous act had reached the end of its ten year period. My memory does not serve me at the moment but I think two, if not three extensions were granted before the final revision was made.
I know that sometimes, in speaking from memory and on the spur of the moment, one is apt to have in his mind, and unintentionally to convey, an impression which may be inaccurate. The Prime Minister quite evidently had in mind that there had been a postponement at one time, but he was mistaken in assuming it was the last time the Bank Act was revised. As a matter of fact there was very strong opposition to any postponement of the 1923 revision. An effort was made by some hon. members in the far corner of the
1Mr. Mackenzie King.]
house to bring about such a postponement. The Right Hon. W. S. Fielding was Minister of Finance at the time. He strongly opposed any postponement. Hon. A. K. Maclean, now a judge of the exchequer court, was chairman of the banking and commerce committee at that time, and during the meetings of that committee he took an equally strong stand against any postponement. Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, who at the time was leading the opposition, took the same position. I shall not take up the time of the house to give the reasons advanced by those hon. gentlemen as to why there should be no postponement, but those reasons would be equally applicable at the present time. The main reason was the importance of settling, at the time contemplated by parliament, all questions that might arise with respect to the banking situation.
The first complete Bank Act was enacted in 1871. It was revised in 1881, again in 1891 and again in 1901. It was with regard to the 1911 revision that a postponement was made, for the reason that 1911 was the year of the coronation of His Majesty King George, and an imperial conference was being held in London which Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then Prime Minister, was expected to attend. It was found necessary to adjourn parliament for a couple of months in order to permit Sir Wilfrid Laurier to go to London to attend the conference and be present at the coronation, and in those circumstances, it being doubtful whether after the coronation there would be time to have the revision effected, Mr. Fielding arranged for a postponement for a year. Before the end of the year the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier was defeated, and a new administration headed by Sir Robert Borden came into office. That government asked for a further postponement of a year .on the ground that they had just come into office and that there were some important matters in connection with the banking situation in Canada which the Minister of Finance, Sir Thomas White, wished to consider. So a postponement was made for another year. That was the only other time at which a postponement was made. The reasons, in both instances, were quite exceptional, but so far as I can see no such reasons exist at the present time.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the government is simply postponing grappling with this among a good many other important questions. Last session we had every reason to hope that there would be a full consideration of the currency question by some committee of this

Bank Act-Mr. Pouliot
house, but the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) pleaded very eloquently for a postponement of that consideration until after the Imperial conference had been held in Canada; he said that the question would be taken up at that conference, and that in the light of the discussion there we would be in a better position to act than by going ahead at the time. When the conference was held this matter received very little discussion, and as a result there was nothing to report afterwards to this parliament. Then there was the question of unemployment insurance. Hon. gentlemen opposite suggested that it would be well to postpone consideration of that question until a dominion-provincial conference was held, but when that conference was held the matter was not discussed at any length, and again there was nothing to report to the house. Again, a few days ago we were discussing the all-important question of reciprocity. We were asked to drop that discussion again because of a pending world conference though an opportunity it was said would be given a little later to discuss it more fully. In the meantime, however, the government received an invitation from the United States, and apparently at the instance of the United States they have begun to take up that question.
It seems to me that here again we have very much the same thing, an effort to get away from dealing with the question at the instance of or by our own parliament, by postponing it to another session. Since the speech from the throne was delivered the government has announced to parliament that it intends to appoint a royal commission to deal with monetary questions, evidently to sit between now and the next session of parliament. I have no doubt that this will be urged as an additional reason why we should not proceed at the present time with this matter, though that was not one of the reasons advanced at the outset.
I should like to make just one remark with reference to that royal commission and what its relation to this revision of the Bank Act may be. Undoubtedly the house will be pleased to see such full consideration of montetary and banking questions as a well qualified royal commission may be prepared to give, but I think it should be distinctly understood that the royal commission in no sense will be a substitute for parliament, and in particular for this House of Commons, in the discussion and ultimate decision on what may be best in banking, currency and other financial matters. Let the commission obtain
as much as possible in the way of relevant information to be placed at the disposal of hon. members, but let it be distinctly understood that when it comes to the revision of the Bank Act itself it will be the judgment of hon. members of this house, in the light of all the information that can be placed before them, rather than the recommendations of any royal commission that will govern parliament in dealing with the matter.

This bill
deals with one of the most important matters affecting the Dominion of Canada, and I naturally expected that the Minister of Finance would have had something to say in support of it. Seeing, however, that apparently he is not going to speak, or has not spoken so far, I shall have to precede him.
I was quite interested in the account given by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) of the various revisions of the Bank Act since confederation, particularly with respect to the investigation which was held in 1923, with the revision that took place at that time; and I was also interested in what the right hon. gentleman had to say regarding the attempt made by members in this corner on that occasion to have the revision postponed for a year. The reason we asked for a postponement was that we felt that no adequate investigation had been held into the needs of Canada so far as the banking system was concerned, or as to what reforms might be brought about in that system to make it more adaptable to our requirements at that time. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF CHARTERS FOR ONE YEAR-POSTPONEMENT OF REVISION
speechtext: Was it not on the score of legislation with respect to rural credits, which my hon. friends wished to have considered first?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF CHARTERS FOR ONE YEAR-POSTPONEMENT OF REVISION
speechtext:
I do not think it was with
regard to legislation affecting rural credits particularly, because that was a separate matter. The experience of Canada during the last ten years has proved, I think, that it would have been a very good step for the government in 1923 to have had a thorough investigation into the question of credits, banking and currency, foreign exchange and all related matters. The result might have been beneficial to us at this time. During the last two or three years we have been drifting along in financial and monetary difficulties. I do not think the world has ever, at least in modern times, experienced such a severe economic depression as we have had in the last few years. It has affected Canada much more seriously than it has some other countries-much more seriously, for example, than it has affected Sweden or Australia or some other places I could name.
[Mr. Speaker.!
The Prime Minister gave us this afternoon an account of bis recent visit to Washington. He told us that monetary as well as economic action is contemplated by the President of the United States, and, as I understood him, he seemed to be in agreement with the president that these two questions must be grappled with together. I suppose that if we are to have any benefit from monetary action with a view to raising price levels it will be granted by every hon. member that this means a measure of inflation, controlled inflation it is true, which is something we in this comer of the house 'have been advocating for a number of years. So far we have not received very much support from the Prime Minister or his followers, and only a year ago the leader of the opposition suggested, with respect to our amendment along this line, that we should wait and see. Well, we have waited and the President of the United States has finally taken action. It seems to me that Canada should be quite prepared to back up the President of the United States and to take the same sort of action here as has been taken in that country.
If we are to have controlled inflation to raise price levels, that certainly suggests some instrument of control. Now, what instrument has Canada whereby to control inflation? I have discussed this matter with economists during the last few years on more than one occasion and have been told that Canada has no proper machinery for controlling inflation to raise price levels to the desired point. It can be done, they said, through controlled inflation, but we have not the proper machinery. If that is true it is not the fault of members in this corner, because in 1924 we endeavoured to have an investigation made into the question of a central bank for Canada. The matter was brought up in 1926 on a motion made from this comer, again in 1928, and in 1931 I myself placed before the house a resolution asking for a central bank in this country. The Prime Minister, if I remember rightly, said in 1931, that the time might come when Canada would need a central bank but that that time had not yet arrived. In my opinion the time had arrived in 1931, and I believed the Prime Minister should then have set to work to establish a central bank. Had this been done we should now have the proper machinery to give us inflation and to control it, in order to raise price levels. It is essential that someone should control it.
I regret that we have not before this established a central bank in this country, but I do not want to be understood now as

Bank Act-Mr. Coote
opposing measures for controlled inflation to raise price levels, even though we have not a central bank; I think we should embark upon that program even in the absence of such a bank.	We should not
however wait any longer. We should establish a central bank now. We can of course have a measure of inflation through the further issue of dominion notes, but this is difficult because of the provisions of the Dominion Notes Act under which we should be obliged to place an additional dollar of gold in the treasury for every additional dollar's worth of notes issued, unless they were issued under the Finance Act which would permit such issue without more gold behind the notes. If, however, we are to have inflation through the Finance Act it can be done only through the chartered banks, and our banks, according to their public statements, do not approve of inflation. I have not yet seen a public utterance of one of our bankers in favour of it, but I have seen a great many public utterances in which they are absolutely opposed to inflation, whether controlled or uncontrolled. Of course, they may change their minds as they have done before.
All through this depression I have been struck by this fact, that our banks have not suggested any way out of the difficulty, at least so far as I know. I am in hearty agreement with the hon. member for East Essex (Mr. Morand), who is reported as having said at Windsor last winter:
A number of our guardians of wealth-for that is what they really are-have made statements in the last few months, and in the last few weeks especially, and I have searched in vain through all their statements, whether of banks or individuals, for one single positive lead. They have simply taken upon themselves the task of giving negative information. They have told us. "Don't do this," and "Don't do that," but I have not been able to find in a single instance a ray of hope that they were trying to work out some solution of our problem.
Inasmuch as our financial leaders are apparently sterile of thought, the some of us who are not financial leaders will have to try and evolve for ourselves some means of getting out of this morass.
One is not entitled to call another man's medicine nostrums and quackery if one hasn't a remedy of his own. It looks to me that our financial leaders are devoting their efforts to finding fault.
I thank the minister for the statement he made on that occasion-or rather the hon. member; I think he is a minister too. Has he not been a minister at some time?

speechtext: He should be.

speechtext: Yes, indeed, and if it were not for the high regard in which I hold the present Minister of Finance I would suggest that the hon. member for East Essex should not have been overlooked.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF CHARTERS FOR ONE YEAR-POSTPONEMENT OF REVISION
speechtext: Speak for yourself.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF CHARTERS FOR ONE YEAR-POSTPONEMENT OF REVISION
speechtext:
I do not wish to indict the bankers; it would not be fair. There are some bankers who do not agree with what I might call the orthodox attitude of the banks towards the depression, but the great majority of them have not come forward with any solution, nor have they given any reason why this depression should continue for three or four years. I remember reading two years ago a report of the proceedings of the annual meeting of one of the Canadian banks. As near as I can remember the matter, the first official who spoke attributed the depression to over-production. The gentleman who followed him said that the way out was to work harder. It is no wonder, if that is the advice we have followed, we have not succeeded in getting out of the depression, and if we follow the advice of orthodox bankers, we shall never get out of it. The bankers want us to pay our debts, but. they do not realize that unless they keep on making loans to some people, the public will not have any money with which to pay their debts. Whether debts can be paid depends upon price levels; debts must be paid out of production and, as I say, whether they can be paid depends on the price which the producers receive for their products. That is simply common sense. The amount of money available in Canada is the chief determining factor in fixing price levels. I know some bankers will not agree with me when I say that the amount of money we have available depends on the action of the banks, but in this regard I shall quote the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, former Chancellor of the Exchequer and at present chairman of the Midland Bank of London. He says:
The amount of money varies only with the action of the hanks in increasing or diminishing deposits. We know how this is effected. Every bank loan and every bank purchase of securities creates a deposit and every repayment of a bank loan and every bank sale destroys one. . . . Bank loans and their repayment, bank purchases and sales are in substance the sole causes of variation in the amount of our money.
I find that opinion corroborated by a writer in the financial

speechtext:
I would point out that
this is a motion for the second reading of a bill to continue bank charters for a year, and as such it does not permit a general discussion of banking or how banks should be run.
Bank Act-Mr. Coote

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF CHARTERS FOR ONE YEAR-POSTPONEMENT OF REVISION
speechtext:
With all due respect, sir,
we are now considering a bill to continue bank charters for a period of one year, and I am discussing the attitude and actions of the banks during the past ten years. Surely that should be a determining factor whether this bill should be passed renewing bank charters for another year. I cannot see that I am out of order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF CHARTERS FOR ONE YEAR-POSTPONEMENT OF REVISION
speechtext: It is out of order to quote opinions from various people as to whether the Canadian system of banking is correct or not, as the question is whether this bill should be passed extending for one year the charters of the banks.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF CHARTERS FOR ONE YEAR-POSTPONEMENT OF REVISION
speechtext:
The gentleman whom I
quoted was not criticising the banks, but even if he were, I think I should be quite in order in quoting him in a debate as to whether bank charters should be renewed for a year. If that is not in order, what would be in order in discussing this bill?
The point I want to make is that the amount of money which we have in Canada determines price levels and the amount of money which we are going to, have depends upon the action of the banks. Surely that is a point which may be discussed when we are deciding whether we shall renew bank charters for a year. If that is out of order, I shall not have anything further to say, because I cannot see that anything else has any more bearing on the matter of whether the charters should be renewed.
A writer in the financial section of the New York Times-and I shall quote only two sentences from him-says in regard to the question where the amount of money comes from and bank deposits:
These include the sums in the ordinary checking accounts of individuals and firms and also include deposits of municipalities, states and counties. They are in part created by making loans; when a bank makes a loan to a customer it does not ordinarily pass out cash, but rather credits the customer with a deposit equal to the loan. In brief, contrary to the common understanding, the bank does not loan out deposits; it loans them in.
I would say that that is contrary to the opinion of many of our leading Canadian bankers and that is one reason I might be justified in expressing concern about renewing their charters for a year, when they do not know any more about the system they are running than is shown by some of their statements on this matter.
The money available for the people of Canada to transact their business with, which money, as I say, is the main factor in determining price levels in this country, has been
[Mr Speaker.]
reduced in the last three years; in other words, bank loans have been reduced from $1,856,000,000 to $1,278,000,000. That shows a reduction of approximately one-third. The reason I am bringing this to the attention of the house is that the bankers themselves-and I think I could quote some of their statements if I had them at hand-claim that has nothing to do with prices. In fact, one writer, in criticizing me, says that the drop in prices is responsible for the deflation of money in Canada. Searoely a week passes but some outstanding banker takes it upon himself to deliver a lecture to our statesmen, our politicians, our various governments, to tell them that they should practise economy, balance their budgets and reduce their expenditures to where it is within their income. It is too bad that the expenditures of our banks are not given the same publicity as are those of our governments. We do not know what happens in Canada, but we have recently had an illustration of what happens in the United States and we are accustomed nowadays to go there for a number of our ideas. I noticed in the New York Times yesterday a dispatch from New York which states:
The income tax authorities in the United States claim that Mr. Mitchell, the ex-president of the National City Bank of New York had a gross income of $3,649,623 in 1929, of which $1,872,861 was in salaries from the National City Bank and the National City Company.
Surely no one man can earn that amount of money from his services to one institution. It is too bad that some of our banks do not practise economy in their head offices and that some of them do not tell us the salaries they are paying there.
The Rank Act should be considered in conjunction with the Finance Act, because our banks rely very largely upon the operations of the Finance Act. All hon. members are, I think, familiar with the fact that the government may advance to the banks without limit against almost any class of security, making the advance in the form of dominion notes. The trustees of the central gold reserve may make a valuation of those securities for the treasury board and the trustees are the three big banks plus the Royal Trust Company which is a subsidiary of one of the banks. In this way the banks have a very powerful influence in the matter of monetary policy and for that reason I am rather concerned that the Bank Act should be renewed for one year without our knowing Whether the banks are willing to cooperate with the government in bringing in a measure of controlled inflation to raise price levels, a thing

Bank Act-Mr. Coote
which the Prime Minister told us this afternoon was so necessary.
I have not time to go into the question of a central bank. I do not want to delay the house too long, because the question has been discussed here before. We should have a central bank to enable us to control inflation for the definite purpose of raising and then stabilizing price levels. Presidents of the Bankers' Association on two occasioans admitted before our committee that they never took that matter into consideration when they were granting credits. To-day it is generally admitted that the amount ^ of credit available is the greatest determining factor in raising or lowering price levels. I would suggest that anyone who is interested should read the evidence given before the banking committee and particularly in 1928 when the president of the Bankers' Association made a very frank admission that they had given no consideration to the effect of their credit policy on price levels.	_
Just before I sit down, I should like to point out to the house that Mr. Roosevelt's action at Washington stands out, I think, in very broad contrast to the action and the attitude which this government has exhibited during the last two years. He has swung his country off the gold standard; he has come out frankly for a policy of controlled inflation. It is worth noting that the main measure under which this inflation _ is imposed is an amendment to the farm relief bill. We have suggested for two or three years that the way to help the farmer is to have a measure of controlled inflation, and we have been told that that would not conform to this country's policy of sound money. How is the sound money policy of this government going to be affected by this policy of the United States? Is our money still going to be sound, or may we not now frankly adopt the same measures which have been proposed by President Roosevelt in the United States. The president has been authorized to issue three billions of new currency, printing press money, and the people of the United States will be glad to get it. The Canadian people during the last two or three years would also have been glad to use two or three hundred million of printing press money, just as the people of the United States -will be glad to use this printing press money in that country.	_
It is proposed under another bill in the United States to issue three billion dollars of government bonds to finance public works, and under another measure to grant five hundred million dollars direct to the
different states for unemployment relief, those funds to be an outright federal donation to the various states. There is a complete justification, I submit, of the financial measures which we have been suggesting from this comer of the house during the last two years for the relief of agriculture and for dealing with the problem of unemployment.
I am not going to take up the time of the house any longer except to say that I do regret that the government has not held an investigation during either of the last two years and by now it could have been prepared to bring down a Bank Act in conformity with the needs of Canada. We brought in a resolution last year asking for an investigation by the banking committee of this house. That committee might very well have been set to work last year and have brought in a report to the house upon which a new act could have been based and introduced this year, or a commission might very well have been appointed last year.
I am very glad that the government has annnounced that they will appoint a royal commission. I hope that when that commission is appointed it will be composed of men who will make a thorough study of the question, that it will not be composed, as I said before, of orthodox Canadian bankers or of some of their hired economists because, if it is, the money spent on it will be thrown away. It is time that we had an investigation by men who, so far as the money and banking end of it is concerned, are free and not directly interested. I should like to see on that commission persons who really represent the people who are most affected by our banking policy. Ir. Canada unfortunately we have left all financial policy in the hands of the banks. If they decide to create more money and more credit we shall have more to do our business with, and there will be more business and better prices. On the other hand if they decide to contract, it is just too bad for the people, but it will happen nevertheless. I do hope that when the commission is appointed men will be chosen who are independent in the sense I have mentioned, and that the government will appoint some men who are outstanding in the field of economics in the old country and in Canada as well.
I am not going to oppose this bill in any way. At this late stage I suppose we must pass the bill as it is presented, but I do hope that the commission which the government will appoint will be such that their work
Bank Act-Mr. Coote

will be of real value and will enable us to improve our banking system and to provide purchasing power sufficient to enable us to make better use of our resources and thereby improve our standard of living. That is the great problem of business to-day, and it is not going to be solved by the world economic conference, because that is a domestic problem. The work of the banks is chiefly domestic. The matter of controlling foreign exchange I submit should be in the hands of a central bank, and I was very glad to notice that in the speech which the Prime Minister made in Toronto some time ago he rather indicated that the time had arrived when we should at least consider the establishment of a central bank in Canada. I hope that he is favourably inclined to that suggestion, and that he will give to the appointment of this royal commission the very greatest care.
Just one other thought which comes to me, and which I should like to express before I sit down. I hope the rumour which I have heard is not correct, that after this commission has done its work and presented its report it is the intention of the government to have the new Bank Act brought in by way of the Senate and referred to a Senate committee, so that it will not be necessary to refer it to a committee of the House of Commons. That is a practice which is becoming altogether too common. I do not like it at all. It was done last year in connection with the Insurance Act. It was done this year in connection with the Railway Act and the Shipping Act, all very important bills. I do not, think the House of Commons should allow that practice to grow, and especially when it comes to the Bank Act the elected representatives of the people should compose the committee to which- the bill will be referred before it comes up for consideration by this house.

speechtext:
I
should like to say a word before the second reading carries by way of concurring in the observations made by the last speaker (Mr. Coote).

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF CHARTERS FOR ONE YEAR-POSTPONEMENT OF REVISION
speechtext: Are you joining up?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF CHARTERS FOR ONE YEAR-POSTPONEMENT OF REVISION
speechtext:
I have no objection to joining up on that particular principle, whatever objections I might have on other principles. It appears to me that there is nothing more important to the people of this country than the postponement of the revision of the Bank Act. The operations of the banks are so mixed up with business generally that I do not believe there is any possibility of our business 
rising from the depressed state in which it is unless there is some reform of the abuses with which our Bank Act teems. Every business in Canada directly or indirectly is connected with the banks. In fact, I have heard it stated with some degree of authority that from fifty to seventy-five per cent of our business enterprises and our commerce are in the hands of the banks; so that if we propose to revive business the first step should be taken by going to the fountainhead, the banks themselves. The workers, the farmers and the business men of this country are all concerned in the Bank Act of Canada to a greater or less degree because owing to the ramifications of this act or to the manoeuvres of those who operate it they may be face to face with starvation or with a loss of their employment. I do not think it is going too far to say that a great deal of the distress which exists in Canada to-day is due to the harsh and ruthless policy of deflation which has been followed by the banks. I would suggest that the policy of governments to-day should be to reverse the process which we have been undergoing, and instead of carrying on the inflation of the banks and the deflation of the public, we should inflate the public and deflate the banks just as the public have been deflated.
The Bank Act was instituted and certain privileges were given to the banks in order that they might be of service to the people. But the contrary has been the case. Instead of becoming the servants of the people the banks have become their masters. There is hardly anyone in this country who is not in some way or other working for the banks. I leave it to any business man in this house, to any professional man, almost to any labour man, if he is not working for the banks, and I might almost add that the government and the House of Commons are working for the banks.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext:
And getting paid
nothing for it.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF CHARTERS FOR ONE YEAR-POSTPONEMENT OF REVISION
speechtext:
At the present time we are working for nothing, and may quite possibly thank the banks who will not let the government pay us any money. I suggest that a great many matters which come before us for ratification, such as orders in council, are passed directly in the interests of the banks.
I suggest that if the government, through orders in council, has guaranteed certain loans to the wheat pools it was in the interests of the banks. I suggest that if the Manitoba savings office losses were guaranteed, it was in the interest of the banks. I suggest that if at the present time we find ourselves in an unfortunate position, so far as our railway com-

Bank Act-Mr. Power
parties are concerned, it is because this country went into the railway business in order to save the credit of the banks. I suggest we have gone to the assistance of the dominion of Newfoundland-which was none of our business-in order to assist two or three Canadian banks. I am not sufficiently familiar with banking and its ramifications to be able to say, as has been said, that we have the finest banking system in the world. I am not attacking the soundness of our banks, because I do not know whether or not they are sound. I believe that under our legislation it would be impossible in any case for the banks to fail and, that at the present time they have their coffers filled with documents, which the Prime Minister called promissory notes, of municipalities, provinces and possibly of the dominion.

Since that time may I add that the situation has changed, not for the better but for the worse. Hon. members will note that the loans to general stores, sundry wholesalers and retailers, those people who carry on the business which represents the life blood of Canadian commerce, have been decreased by'51-5 per cent. Those are the figures as of February 1932. Since that time I say the situation has been greatly aggravated. I have not the figures before me, and I do not know whether
or not as yet they have been analyzed. The statement I have read deals only with the Canadian Bank of Commerce. But I would say that the loans to public institutions must have increased by May 1933 by at least thirty-five or forty per cent, and the decrease in loans to ordinary businesses, to traders, to the lumbering industry and to every other primary industry of Canada must have been enormous.
For those reasons I believe there should have been initiated at this session a complete study of our whole banking situation. I have no objection to the appointment of a royal commission. Such a commission could have supplemented the efforts of a committee of the house, and no doubt would have been of great assistance in giving technical advice.
I fear, however, as does the hon. member who has just spoken, that in the composition of the royal commission those people most vitally interested in the banking situation will not be represented. The farmers, the small merchants, the workers-all these have suffered through a policy of excessive deflation carried on by Canadian banks. I fear that those people will not be represented, and further, that they will be unable to make their representations to the commission. It is very difficult for a man, who has hanging over his neck the threat that the bank can close him up next day, to appear before a commission and explain the situation as he sees it. I fear that the commission may tour the country from one end to the other and that those who are really in need of assistance through a revision of the Bank Act will not be heard, will be unable to have their views placed before and dealt with by the commission. Having made this statement, with the reservation that when the report comes in next year I hope hon. members will be permitted to use their own judgment and discretion as to the manner in which they will deal with it, and as to whether or not they will accept its recommendations, I desire to protest again against the postponement of the revision of the Bank Act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been deeply interested in the remarks of the hon. members for Macleod (Mr. Coote) and Quebec South (Mr. Power). I do not rise at this time to object to the bill, because I believe we have gone too far in the session to be in a position to take any action whatsoever with regard to the revision of the Bank Act.
I should like to remind the house, however, that in 1923 when the present member for
Bank Act-Mr. Spencer

Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) introduced a resolution asking for an investigation into the basis of credit, its function and control and its relation to trade, we had a very interesting and valuable investigation. After the investigation had taken place many hon. members from this corner of the house together with other hon. members who sat on the committee, did their best to have the revision of the Bank Act postponed for one year, so that we would have an opportunity of going into the evidence which had been submitted not only by important witnesses from different parts of Canada, but by witnesses from the United States and Great Britain. We tried to secure a postponement at that time because we realized that a great deal of valuable information had been given, and that we would not be in a position to make proper use of it unless we had an opportunity for study. We were not given that opportunity. The committee was forced to go on with the revision of the Bank Act, and to say the least that revision was forced through as fast as possible.
Now that the government has decided to have a royal commission to investigate the problem of banking and finance I hope the same condition will not arise. I trust we will not be asked to go on with the revision of the Bank Act as soon as the report is presented. I hope the commission will get to work at an early date, that they will do their work thoroughly and that the report will be in the hands of the members in time to give ample opportunity to study it before we take up the revision of the Bank Act in 1934. If it is possible to have the report in our hands before parliament meets, all the better. If not I submit we should have it very early in the session, and that members of the banking and commerce committee at least will be given an opportunity to study that report before we go on to the next part of our business in connection with the Bank Act.
In studying the Bank Act next year I think not only should particular consideration be given to the problems of financing railways, fisheries, forestry, mining and industries generally, but I would point out that as far as the basic industry of this country is concerned, agriculture; the present banking system is about the poorest form of financing that industry could possibly have. I do not particularly blame these private institutions for not wanting to have much to do with agriculture, at the present time particularly, but the fact remains that, the industry has to be financed. If we have a banking system that

prides itself on making only short term lqans for two, three and four months, when agriculture needs loans for at least six to twelve months and sometimes two or three years, and as the private banking system charges that industry the highest rate of interest, eight or nine per cent and sometimes more, it stands to reason that the industry has no chance to succeed. Therefore when the Bank Act comes up for revision we should see that arrangements are made that the banking system will finance agriculture suitably, or if it cannot we should find other ways and means of financing it. It is not necessary for me to go over the wide field covered so well by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote). I would only repeat in regard to deflation that whenever we deflate by a certain amount we increase debts to an equal amount. Otherwise, in halving prices we double debts.
Banks to-day are too inflexible. We had some very interesting information given us in 192S when we had an investigation in the banking and commerce committee on that point. Banks may inflate or deflate against the interests of the country. We have to recognize that our monetary system is made up of three parts largely; the minted money, the printed money and the written money. We all recognize to-day that the written money, that based on ledger entries, and drawable by cheque, is over 90 per cent of the money we use. As the hon. member for Macleod reminded us, this money is brought into being through the action of the banks in making loans, which in turn increase deposits. I have in my hand a statement showing that deposits in 1922 amounted to $1,192,000,000. The actual cash at that time in subsidiary coin and notes was $229,000,000. In a speech made by Mr. Jackson Dodds, general manager of the Bank of Montreal before the board of trade in Winnipeg in March last, he stated that they made their loans from preexisting savings deposits, I wonder how he got that understanding. We find that, although we only had $1,192,000,000 in 1922, we increased that by 1929 to $1,480,000,000, and we also increased the amount of notes and subsidiary cash from $229,000,000 to $247,000,000 in the same time. Apparently he has another guess coming. We all know that in good times the banks compete in making loans; in bad times they compete in forcing collections and destroying purchasing power. Yet they say competition is the life of trade. I would remind hon. members of the truth we all know so well, that directly we start to curtail credit, which curtailment is brought about by the banking system, we at once have a crash in

Bank Act-Mr. Bennett
prices, and that at once reacts on unemployment and the army of the unemployed begins to grow.
It is not necessary I think for me to refer at length to the Finance Act, that also has been touched upon. However, I would like to remind hon. members that the Finance Act is more or less like a slot machine. When a bank brings securities to it, it gets dominion notes on a safe margin, and I have yet to find any limitation. We have been told until we are tired of hearing it that Canada's banking system is the soundest in the world. If it is not it ought to be, when it has the government of Canada behind it. If the banks of this country, being private institutions, can at any time bring securities to the treasury board under the Finance Act and get dominion notes for them, surely the country supports the banks. Therefore if the country is sound the banking system ought to be sound also.
If, when the commission does sit, inquiry is made of it as to the advisability of starting a central bank, it will recommend that a central bank be formed, as has been suggested so many times from different parts of this house. I see no reason why a central bank should not do a great deal of good in taking care of all government business. Why should it not take over the work carried on to-day by the treasury board? Why should it not take over the work of the central gold reserve? Why should it not buy and sell securities and so help to regulate the price level? Why should it not buy and sell foreign exchange? Why should it not have a monopoly of note issue? Is there any other business in Canada that as soon as it is given a licence to live has the huge privilege of being able to double its capital at the cost of printing and paper, a privilege we give the banking institutions? Lastly why should not the central bank be a depository for the total amount of money in our post office savings offices? These are some things that it seems to me that a central bank might do. Therefore in saying these few words in regard to this bill I hope that when investigation is made into this whole problem the members of this parliament, and particularly the members of the banking and commerce committee, will be given full opportunity and plenty of time to study the report before being asked to review the Bank Act in 1934.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one has to go away from home to realize fully the value of the institutions of one's own country. As I listened this afternoon I did not intend to participate in this debate. But when I heard the attack
made on our institutions, heard them held up to scorn as they were, I recalled a conversation of, I think, five days ago in which I was assured that if the banking institutions of the great republic beside us had been similar to our own they would not have experienced the difficulties that they have.
I was rather surprised at the statement of the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) that we as a government had not taken the initiative in connection with these matters as had been done by the President of the United States. Well, Mr. Speaker, the United States had no option. Their banks all closed; they had to, because the system was defective for this reason:	They could lend money without limitation as to the character of the security upon which it was loaned. Having loaned money upon real estate in large amounts these depositors-who were not paper depositors or transfer ledger depositors, to whom the hon. gentleman has referred so often that it would be amusing if it were not so tragic-wanted their money, but when they drew their cheques for the money the banks could not meet those cheques because they had put the money into real estate mortgages. It became so serious that in the end every bank in the United States was closed.
I confess to being one of those who did not think the time would ever come when all the banks in the city of New York would close. When the governor of Michigan closed the banks in that state it became inevitable that the banks in the central west would close also, because in a general way we knew the character of the securities they held for their deposits, but I did not think the banks in New York would close. However, they did close. Who will compare for a moment at this time and under those circumstances the financial institutions of our country with those of the richest country in the world? I can assure this house-and I agree with the hon. gentleman who made the statement- that while one does not desire to talk about Canada having the finest banking institutions in the world, I do say that we have come thus far through a great crisis with singular credit to Canadian banking institutions. I will go that far. I may say also in reply to the right hon. gentleman, who suggested that we have been dilatory in dealing with thtse questions of banking, credit and currency, that in the early fall, when the session was to be called to deal with the agreements, the government discussed the matter very carefully not only among its members but with others as well, trying in a large sense to
Bank Act-Mr. Bennett

Bank Act-Mr. Bennett

opposite will have an opportunity to make their statement. It is no use quoting what Reginald McKenna or somebody else in London says about conditions in Canada. This country has peculiar problems, questions that are quite different from those of most countries. Here we have half a continent inhabited by about 10,000,000 people, and when you think they are carrying on operations so that they ocupy the fifth or sixth trading position in the world, you begin to realize the magnitude of the problem with which we have to deal. It is important too- and I trust every member of parliament will see to this-that the representations made to that commission will be made by those who have an intimate knowledge of the concrete working of our banking system. It is no use saying that banks charge 8 per cent when they should charge only 7 per cent. That only shows that this is a departure from the provisions of the statute. That is not the point. The point is whether or not we have taken by our legislation appropriate steps, shall I say, to safeguard, not only the interests of the depositors-and the shareholders-they of course have little or no stake in that phase of the matter because their -money is locked up in bank premises and the specie that is held by the bank; if you will take the trouble to ascertain, you will see that-but the business of Canada. Banking in a large way is the business of Canadians. I have given much attention myself and so have my colleagues as to the personnel of that commission. If I were in a position to announce it to the house now, when we are seeking an extension of the Bank Act for another year, I would do so. It is perfectly clear that we must not confine it entirely to Canadians; that is obvious. On the other hand, it is important that its personnel should be such as would ensure knowledge on the part of the commission as a whole of the practical workings of our banking system. In other words, I think the banking interests should be represented at least for that purpose. Then you must have representation for those who are concerned in the working of the banking system as the users of it, not the makers of it, and above all we must endeavour, and shall endeavour, to ensure that those who direct the commission will see to it that an opportunity is given to everybody who so desires to speak with respect to banking from the standpoint of the country as a whole.
I think perhaps it is not fair to say that in any sense have we endeavoured to escape the responsibility that rests upon us because, barring accidents, in all probability the same government would be here in 1934, and they

would have to accept the responsibility. So it was not for the purpose of escaping responsibility at all that the -revision of the Bank Act was postponed but for the reasons that I have given to the house-an earnest desire to do what we conceived might be the best for the purposes of this country as a whole.
When -the ho-n. gentleman referred to the assistance that was given by the dominion to enable the wheat -pools and the savings banks of Manitoba or Newfoundland to function, when an hon. gentleman said, for instance, that when we gave o-ur guarantee -in connection with the savings bank o-f Manitoba we gave it i-n the interests of the banks, may I hasten to assure -him that we declined absolutely to consider the proposition until there were 40,000 depositors who had in their possession books under which -they were entitled, by custom rather than by the strict word of the contract, to write a cheque against that savings bank in Manitoba and against which there was not a single -thing left in the till except the rattle of -the I.O.U's. That was the position that induced us to take the step we did.
I am not going to go over the ground again with respect to the wheat pool operations. On Friday last the United States farm board, which had been dealing with the wheat problem, closed out their business after -they had made a loss of $160,000,000, an-d had given twenty-eight million bushels of wheat to the Red -Cross for distribution. Their loss on cotton is well known to this house. I shall not do more than say, with respect to our loans to provinces, that on Friday last the state o-f New York received from the Reconstruction Finance Corporation $9,000,000, bringing its total loans to $29,000,000, and Missouri and California were in the same position. What we have been doing the United States is only just beginning to do. With respect to the $500,000,000, to which the bon. member for Macleod referred, I do not think it has yet been settled that that is to -be a gift, but just for the purpose of aiding employment in the states. That is the -method that is to be -pursued for -the purpose of maintaining the autonomous position of the states, just as we have done of the provinces. Such assistance is being given by -reason of the national character of the disaster in ord-er to ensure that all shall be in some small way protected.
I trust that in giving the second reading to this bill to extend the period within which the -bank charters will operate for another yea-r the house will realize that the govern-

Bank Act-Mr. Ralston
ment does it with a full sense of the responsibility that rests upon it and with an earnest desire on the part of the administration to provide facilities by which the Canadian people, speaking as a whole through the commission, may have an opportunity upon the evidence there adduced to report to those best able, best able I say, to make such recommendations to this house as will clothe the members of this house with that knowledge which is essential to arrive at a sound judgment or conclusion with respect to this matter.
May I, without being offensive, suggest that moderation in matters of this kind is desirable. When sometimes our statements made in this house with respect to our institutions are carried abroad, and our people are denounced in the terms in which they sometimes are, it must be remembered that the banks of this country are controlled in the end by the people who deposit their moneys with them. In other words, it is confidence that is entirely behind the maintenance of the structure of our banks. I said the other evening something about confidence plus being the important thing. The real fact is that since then the nations of the world are endeavouring to discover how they may be able to establish some method for controlling international exchange, using the word in the broadest possible sense, including moneys and commodities, and with respect to the one, when the hon. gentleman referred to the history of the United States in connection with its so-called inflation, the truth is that that republic is so rich, holding nearly half the gold of the world, that no method so far yet practised has reduced the value of its paper below one hundred cents on the dollar, nor is it apt to. You cannot quite say that with respect to anything else except perhaps the gold franc at something less than four cents. You have there an illustration of the value of confidence. They have the backbone of assets, real assets, assets of gold, which is the international medium or measure. On the other hand you have other communities, strong, vigorous, with great futures before them, but they have not the same assets immediately available for the purpose of giving that confidence which is essential in international transactions.
I can only ask this house and every member of it to look upon this measure for the revision of the Bank Act as something far greater than any mere party question. Any suggestion that may be made for permitting the representations of various members to be 53719-281 j
heard before that commission in order that every school of thought may find adequate expression will certainly not only be favourably considered by the administration but every effort will be made to see that those views are thus expressed.

speechtext:
I rise, Mr. Speaker, to make a very few observations and to bring the house back to what is after all the question before the chair, and that is whether the charters of the banks shall be renewed for another year, notwithstanding the provision of the Bank Act which requires that every ten years there shall be a revision.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister has wandered a considerable distance, but I have no doubt he was dealing with what has been said from different parts of the house this afternoon. We want to discuss this matter in moderation, and to meet his suggestion that the discussion be without party bias. But after all the real question is whether or not the government are justified in proposing at this time that the charters of the banks shall be extended for another year notwithstanding the provisions of the Bank Act. Searching my right hon. friend's speech for arguments in support of the proposition I for one, Mr. Speaker, find that he has almost overproved his case; in other words, that he has shown that the banking situation is so sound in this country and the integrity of the banks so unimpeachable, compared with the United States, that there should be no difficulty whatever in proceeding as usual with a revision of the Bank Act instead of postponing it for another year. I am not speaking in a sarcastic manner at all; I mean what I say. The Prime Minister has given every evidence that during his visit to the United States last week he heard such testimonials with respect to our banking system that we would be led to expect there would be no reason in the world why a revision should not be proceeded with in the ordinary way. No reason has been given by the Minister of Finance, and the only reason given by the Prime Minister was the statement at the close of his address that the government- and he took full personal responsibility-having regard to the chaotic conditions in the world, and the disturbance which would be created in our banking institutions, felt it would be inadvisable to revise the Bank Act this year. He did not tell us-and so far as I know it is not so,-that the banks have asked that the postponement be made. This is purely a move on the part of the government, because they feel a little timorous, if I
Bank Act-Mr. Ralston

may express it that way, as to the results, the effects or the possibilities of an inquiry such as would be had before the banking and commerce committee. I do not suggest that the government feel these institutions would not come out quite all right, but at the same time they feel conditions are so distressing that such an inquiry should not be launched. I wish to present the other side of the shield, and to say to the Prime Minister that if the banks of Canada are in the position he suggests-and I have no reason to believe they are not; I would be the last to question the standing of our banking institutions-if the banking institutions are in this position, is it hot the part of reason, wisdom, common sense and orderly administration to go ahead and do business as usual with regard to the Bank Act, and have the revision at the time and in the manner prescribed as has been regularly done in the past. Is it not better to do that, than to postpone revision for another year, on the ground that chaotic conditions and possible dislocations or disturbances to the banking institutions make it unwise to proceed. That is the point which appeals to some hon. members on this side of the house. When the Prime Minister suggests that a royal commission is to be appointed, I remind him, as my right hon. leader has already done, that a royal commission cannot take the place of an inquiry by representatives sent here by the people of Canada, men representing all shades of opinion and all classes. They should examine the monetary, financial and currency questions faoing the country.
I say this to my right hon. friend and his government, that if there were no other reason for proceeding with a revision this year, than to afford a forum where members of this house and where the public could get information and could come face to face with the business leaders, financial men and bankers, a revision of the Bank Act would be justified. At a time like this, when economic conferences are being held in every club and every smoking car, every place where men congregate, when economic questions are constantly under discussion, a revision of the Bank Act would have been very proper and very useful. A great deal of information exchanged is, undoubtedly, misinformation; men are very much misinformed. I believe the world is reaching the point where nobody will boast of having much understanding in connection with these problems, but by meeting men who are expert in these matters and discussing with them economic questions, much good would be gained.
Just at this time, when the revision of the Bank Act is due, in accordance with the ten

year provision, economists the world over are saying that even tariffs and debt settlements must take secondary place to a revision of monetary systems, in order that conditions may be stabilized. The Prime Minister speaks of the situation in the United States and the inflational or reflational action taken by the government of that country. He knows such action has not been taken only because of the situation which arose in connection with banking institutions. He knows it has been taken because of an international situation as well, and because of the position in which the United States found herself on account of her unit of currency being so different from and out of line with the parities in the rest of the world.
Monetary and currency questions are coming to be regarded as an important first step towards a revival of world trade. I submit there could have been no better place for a discussion of those problems, the presentation of all views with respect to them and for the crystallization of ideas and the possible emerging of some definite policies, than in the banking and commerce committee of the House of Commons, assisted, as it would be, by experts who would come before it to give evidence. I submit that by not having that done, the government is losing a great opportunity.
My complaint about the royal commission, outside of the fact that it is not as representative as would be a committee of the House of Commons, is that it is about a year too late. This matter has been before the countries of the world for some time. Men have begun to realize that monetary problems are very important so far as the rehabilitation of the world is concerned. Yet at this time the government does not propose to revise the Bank Act or to take any definite action with respect to the monetary situation; it only proposes to appoint a commission before which people may appear. This, in spite of the fact that in the country to the south of us most drastic and far-reaching action is being taken. I quite admit that those measures may not actually be put into effect, but at least the president of the republic is given power to act along the broadest lines, by way of deflation, or degradation of the gold dollar; by way of the issue, if necessary, of paper currency; by way of the redemption of treasury notes, and so on. Those are measures which would have shocked the world twelve months ago but are being provided for in the country to the south of us at the present time.

Bank Act-Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver)
At this time therefore I rise to join with other hon. members on this side of the house in protesting against the attitude of the government with regard to the Bank Act. We take our position not because we are criticizing these institutions, but because we believe that by proceeding with the revision there would have been an opportunity for this House of Commons to do real work in connection with education and information, and perhaps evolving policies which would have been for the benefit of Canada in the crisis through which she is passing.

This afternoon the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) repeated practically in detail an address which he delivered in this House of Commons in February, 1932. Having a somewhat tenacious memory, during the right hon. gentleman's observations I had the pleasure of reviewing what occurred upon that occasion. To-day we heard the same old shibboleths, the same old time-worn theories as we heard then. We have heard the defence of sound money outlined once again, and the gold mentality, Which is absolutely inseparable from the right hon. gentleman, was once more apparent, as it was in February, 1932. The golden calf was once more trotted out for exhibition before the wondering gaze of the Canadian people.
What were the two objections of the Prime Minister to our daring to criticize the Canadian banking system? He told us in the first place that had the United States had the system Canada has had during the last few years she would not have had the same financial troubles.

I am quite ready to admit that what my right hon. friend has said is true, but he says that it was quite all right for a Liberal government to bring down a measure to extend bank charters for one year because they wanted Canada to be represented at an imperial conference, but it is quite another thing when a Conservative administration brings down a similar proposal with regard to world conference during the worst crisis in the history of the world. The speech from the throne made the situation very clear; it said:
You will be invited to extend Canadian bank charters for one year in order that parliament may be informed of the results of the proposed world economic and financial conference, to be called to consider financial, economic and monetary problems, before undertaking the decennial revision of the Bank Act.

speechtext: That was in the speech from the throne. I have only this to say, Mr. Speaker: I do not profess for a moment to be competent to give an expert or even a fair, average opinion as to what ought or ought not to be done with this or that phase of the proposals with regard to banking and monetary questions. I do submit, however, what has been pointed out by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) that we have in Canada, whatever imperfections it may have, a banking system that has stood the test of the greatest financial storms known dm the history of the world. We must not forget that fact.

speechtext: May I suggest to the hon. gentleman that all he is now saying is that Canada stood the storm and the shocks. All Canada is now behind the banks; we are in the banking business but we have no direct control.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext:
My hon. friend has succeeded in having his opinion placed upon Hansard in the form of a question. I do not object; if he wishes to insert the word Canada I will agree. Canada 'and its financial and banking institutions have weathered the storm. However, I am not going to attempt to discuss the merits of the question. I venture to say that if the government had proceeded in the ordinary course and revised the Bank Aot we would have been subjected to very great criticism for dashing into that revision at a time when we did not have the advantage of the findings of the world economic conference. My hon. friend from Vancouver Centre said he pointed out last year that we should have a royal commission; he agrees that this should be done, but the point he makes is that it is a year late. I will meet that argument by saying to my hon. friend that we have had the benefit of a year's experience, and we are in a much better position to deal with financial affairs in the light of that experience than we would have been a year ago. I am sure the people in the great republic to our south will approach these subjects in a much more chastened frame of mind than would have been the case twelve months ago.
In closing this debate, Mr. Speaker, I merely rose for the purpose of dealing with the question of the propriety of our asking that bank charters should be renewed for a period of one year. I am in perfect accord with the suggestion of the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) that this is the sole subject that should be discussed on the motion for second reading. Having said that much I do not propose to be responsible for delaying the second reading of this bill a moment longer.

Motion agreed to on division, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Gagnon in the chair.
On section 1-Bank charters continued to July 1, 1934.

speechtext:
I have only a few words
to say, Mr. Chairman, because my hon. friend from Quebec South expressed in much better language than my own some of the thoughts I had entertained in regard to this matter. The right hon. Prime Minister spoke of moderation, and I think this is the first time 1 have heard him mention that word in this house. He spoke also about attacks made by the opposition on our financial institutions. May I point out that in the House of Commons members of the opposition may not attack members of the government and vice versa, but regarding matters outside the house any member is at liberty to pass judgment on individuals who have served the government in any capacity; or on institutions, and in doing so he is not attacking anyone but merely exercising his right as a member of parliament to express his views conscientiously on all questions that come before the house.
There are two questions to be considered under this bill; first there is the postponement of the revision of the Bank Aot, and secondly the manner in'which the whole subject is to be investigated in the interval. As regards the postponement of the revision of the act, it seems to me that if the govenment had a strong policy on banking it could very well submit that policy right now. There are two ways of studying this matter; there is a regular way and an irregular. I thank the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) for his support of my view, which is the view of many other hon. members. I think that the whole question should be submitted to a special committee of the house who could hear witnesses and pass judgment on their evidence. That is the regular course, which I think should be adopted. The irregular course is to appoint a royal commission. Who will be appointed no one knows. As my hon. friend from Quebec South has pointed out, it is difficult to select representatives from among the farmers and the small town and village merchants.
Mention has been made to-day of conferences. We have heard that the leader of the government is a superman. Now, those who will meet at the conference in London will be mere men, so that the superman will be very much above them. I remember that after the hon. member for Renfrew had said that Mr. Ferguson was so admirable the hon.

Bank Act
member for St. Ann observed that it was an honour for Mussolini to be compared with the Prime Minister. Well, if the Prime Minister is such an outstanding figure I do not see why he will take the trouble to cross the ocean to attend the world conference; he will meet only pygmies there. It reminds me of the Big Endeins and the Little Enders; he is the Big Ender and he will meet the Little Enders. If he is the superman what is the use of his spending the money of this country to cross the ocean merely in order to meet narrowminded people in London? He can give his views right now from Ottawa. I am sure they would be accepted the world over, and they would not only reflect great credit on himself but would establish his supremacy as the superman.
As regards inflation, I was much interested in the discussion that took place between the hon. member forWevburn (Mr. Young) and my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie). I believe these gentlemen should settle their difficulties between themselves. May I say once more, however, in the presence of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) who is an expert on inflation, that the statement was made by him, in answer to a question I asked some time ago, that if the tariff barriers were lowered there would be no use for inflation. So that if the difficulties in connection with our present monetary and currency system are due to the tariff policy that has been adopted everywhere, it would seem to me that the moment every nation came to its senses and lowered its tariff barriers we ought to hear no more about inflation. If that were brought about I am sure my hon. friend from Macleod would realize how right he was when he answered so conscientiously the question I put to him on that occasion to which I have referred.

The statement was made during the discussion on the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce. He said, "I believe that as soon as tariffs are lowered reasonably there
will be no necessity for inflation." We have the proof of that in the fact that when trade was normal owing to a normal tariff we never heard a word about inflation.

speechtext: The Prime Minister spoke of the terrific losses of the banks in western Canada. I am sorry to hear that. If it is true, I would lay the responsibility directly on the shoulders of the administration who, by their monetary policy, have endeavoured to keep us as near to world gold prices as possible. Their policy has kept prices of the products of the west to the point where the farmers are unable to pay back the loans made by the banks. Had the debt-paying power of wheat been as great in the west during the last two years as in Australia, the farmers would have been able to pay back to the banks a great many millions of dollars which they have been unable to return.
