speechtext:
There are one or two questions I should like to ask the minister in regard to this bill which is to renew the Bank Act for a period of a year. Section 91 of the present act sets a limit of 7 per cent on the rate of interest which a bank may charge.
Bank Act

I just wanted to ask the minister whether he is aware that on many bank loans rates much in excess of 7 per cent are being charged, whether the inspector general of banks ever reports to him in connection with that matter, whether he has heard anything about it and, whether he does not think, before this bill is passed out of committee, some amendment should be made to section 91 so that banks will be compelled to comply with what is admittedly the intention of that section.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF CHARTERS FOR ONE YEAR-POSTPONEMENT OF REVISION
speechtext: Whatever merits the suggestion of my hon. friend may have-and I am not for a moment intimating that there are no merits in it-the fact remains that in a renewal of bank charters for a period of a year we are not attempting in any way to revise the Bank Act. If we started in on the question of amending this, that or the other section of the Bank Act, we would be attempting in committee of the whole house to revise the act without the matter going to the banking and commerce committee; so that his suggestion is not one which we could properly entertain in connection with a bill of this kind.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF CHARTERS FOR ONE YEAR-POSTPONEMENT OF REVISION
speechtext:
When this matter was before the house either last year or the year before-and I think it was last year-the statement was made on more than one occasion by more than one member that the Bank Act would be up for revision this year. Many members admitted that section 91 should be revised so that banks would be compelled to remain within the limit of 7 per cent on loans made by them. Perhaps if I brought to the attention of the minister some of the rates they are charging, he might take more interest in the matter. The rates which I am going to mention are contained in a return which was recently brought down, a return which the banks make under a certain section of the act. In this return the banks are required to show the maximum rates of interest charged on the different classes of loans. They divide these loans into four classes: A, B, C and D. As I remember the matter, class A loans are for any amount up to $250; class B, for amounts from $250 to $1,000; class C, loans from S1.000 to $25,000, and class D, loans over $25,000.
On page 15 of the return brought down there is a class C loan, that is a loan between $1,000 and $25,000, which shows 10 per cent interest being charged on an overdraft. On page 16 of the return, the discount rate charged on a class B loan, that is on an amount between $250 and $1,000, for a period of one month, is shown at 9 per cent. On 
page 17 of the return a rate of 12 per cent is shown on a class B loan, a rate of 10 per cent on a class C loan and a rate of 8 per cent on a class D, that is for an amount over $25,000. On page 18, the return shows a discount rate of 10 per cent on a class B loan, that is an amount between $250 and $1,000, for a period of ninety days and a rate of 10 per cent on a class C loan, that is an amount between $1,000 and $25,000, for a period of ninety-one days. The rates which are shown in this return show clearly the need for revising that section of the act at this session of parliament. The business men and farmers of Canada cannot stand such rates of interest. The banks are taking an unfair advantage -of their customers in charging such rates and that is the reason I am bringing the matter to the attention of the house.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF CHARTERS FOR ONE YEAR-POSTPONEMENT OF REVISION
speechtext:
Does the
return show whether those rates were for loans made in Canada?
Mr. COOTE. I am speaking from memory and I shall have to speak subject to correction, but so far as I remember all the loans I have mentioned were in Canada. I would like to ask the minister whether these rates have been brought to his attention and now that I have brought them to his notice, whether he will not consider amending this one section of the act. Many members, if not a majority of the house, felt last year that a general revision of the act would take place at this session and accordingly the matter was allowed to go over for a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF CHARTERS FOR ONE YEAR-POSTPONEMENT OF REVISION
speechtext: I can only point out again to my hon. friend that we are not amending the Bank Act except to renew the charters for a period of one year. I know quite well that on perusal of the return which my hon. friend received, he would be able to find instances showing a much higher percentage than those he has mentioned, but in most oases they have reference to loans for only a short period, some for only a few days, and the service charge, which is a proper one, I believe, in most cases at least, is included in the rate, thus making it a figure which, without examination, would appear almost fantastic. But I do not think this is the place or the time to enter into a discussion of that or any other aspect of the merits of the Bank Act as such.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF CHARTERS FOR ONE YEAR-POSTPONEMENT OF REVISION
speechtext:
Surely this cannot be referred to in any way as a service charge, nor can it be regarded as fantastic, the rate is 10 per cent on a class B loan, that is a loan from $250 to $1,000, for ninety days. That is a

Bank Act
fair sized loan and for as long a period of time as most banks, according to their own statement, will lend money, yet they are charging 10 per cent when they should be charging only 7 per cent. Something should be done about this matter.
Let me draw the minister's attention to another one. On a loan of over $25,000, a rate of 8 per cent is being charged. On a demand loan of over $1,000 ten per cent is being charged. The instances which I have cited should convince the minister that, in spite of what he says about this not being a revision of the Bank Act but simply an extension, when we are in committee would be a good time to revise section 91. These rates are very unfair. If the minister will not do anything about the matter, I can only express my regret and assure him that I believe a majority of the people of Canada feel he should do something about it.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF CHARTERS FOR ONE YEAR-POSTPONEMENT OF REVISION
speechtext:
Supporting the hon.
member for Macleod, I should like to remind the Minister of Finance that is 1932 I introduced into this house a bill to penalize banks which were charging more than the legal rate of interest of 7 per cent. At that time the committee turned it down with the excuse that the Bank Act was coming up for revision in 1933 and therefore the matter could be dealt with this year. The revision has now been put off for another year and I think the hon. member for MacLeod is quite in order in bringing the matter up on the floor of the house at this time.
I would like to ask the Minister of Finance whether he can give us a definite answer with respect to the question asked him by the hon. member for Macleod; that is, does the inspector general of banks draw his attention to bank charges where there are those exorbitant figures above 7 per cent quoted by the bon. member?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext: When the reply was made last year that the Bank Act would come up for revision this year, that was the ordinary expectation, and but for unusual conditions prevailing at the moment the Bank Act would no doubt now be up for revision. The representations made by the hon. member for Macleod and the hon. member for Battle River would very properly be considered at such a .time. I may say to my hon. friend that while nothing can be done so far as amendment is concerned until the Bank Act itself is up for revision, I shall be very happy to draw the attention of the banks to 'the remarks of my hon. friends.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF CHARTERS FOR ONE YEAR-POSTPONEMENT OF REVISION
speechtext:
I am sorry if that is all the minister is going to do about the matter. I have of course no doubt the banks will be duly advised by their friends in the house or the press gallery of the House of Commons of any remarks which I may make. The minister will not do anything about the rate of interest. I would draw the minister's attention to subsection 4 of section 91 of the Bank Act, which says:
No bank shall directly or indirectly charge or receive any sum whatsoever for the keeping of any account unless such charge is made by express agreement between the bank and the customer.
It has been drawn to my attention that a great many banks in western Canada-I do not know about the east-are insisting that the great majority of their customers should sign such a form. I have recently received a communication from a gentleman in Banff in which he says that the bank manager presented to him the following form and asked him to sign it. The form is addressed ito the Imperial Bank of Canada, and reads:
In consideration of your keeping (at your discretion) a current account in your books in name of the undersigned, I-We hereby authorize you to debit such account with a
monthly charge of $	 See schedule below.
Dated at Banff this 10th day of March, 1933.
Them it says:
Balance under $100 allowed 5 cheques per month.
Balance under $200 allowed 10 cheques per month.
Balance under $300 allowed 15 cheques per month.
Over that number 5 cents per cheque with minimum of 50 cents.
That makes a very heavy charge against an account, five cents for the cheque and three cents for the government stamp, or eight cents for every cheque that is drawn. The customer is compelled to sign that form or have his account discontinued. It might fairly be said that this is a matter to be settled between the bank and the customer. I have no objection to that statement except that the banks on every occasion on which they have been before our committee have said: We are giving to the people in many parts of Canada a good many services, and for those services we should be allowed the privilege of note issue. They also say that they should be allowed to exceed the rate of seven per cent, which is stipulated in section 91. The banks are certainly not giving to the people any very great privileges at the present time. They are lending so little
Bank Act

money that they find it difficult to make their branches pay, and a great many of their customers are forced to pay this charge which I have mentioned.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF CHARTERS FOR ONE YEAR-POSTPONEMENT OF REVISION
speechtext:
I have had dozens of men protest to me against it, mostly small retailers in the town who are issuing a great many cheques. They have drafts coming due which they cannot meet, a good many of them, and they will pay $25 or $30. on these drafts, and the draft is sent back to the head office in Toronto or wherever it may be. The firm in Toronto makes out a new draft for another month, and the customer accepts it and when it becomes due pays off another $25 or $30. That process goes on every month, and these business men feel it a very considerable burden. One man told me, "I have discontinued my account at the bank, and I am keeping my cash, what I have, in the safe, and as my bills come due I go down to the bank and pay them." The banks are not fulfilling the function which they were intended to fulfil, and which I believe the majority of the members think they are fulfilling. They are making the customers pay these charges which they have put on in an endeavour to make their country branches pay their way. It seems to me that if the banks are going to continue to have the privilege of note issue and be allowed to charge rates in excess of seven per cent, and apparently they are for at least this year, they are not treating their customers fairly when they insist on this very high charge for keeping a current account. The result will be that they will educate the people to do without banks after a while. They have closed many banks in western Canada. A case in point is at Lundbreclc. Some farmers who were dealing with the bank at Lundbreck will now have to go to Pincher Creek, which will be in a few cases as much as thirty-five miles from their home. When I took up this . matter with the general manger of the bank in question he said, "These men have nearly all got automobiles, and it will not take them very long to go to Pincher Creek and see their banker once in a while, to renew their notes." But other bankers have told me that many farmers could not afford to run their cars any longer. Few of them have buggies

in these days, and if they have to make a trip of thirty-five miles in a lumber wagon to their bank to renew their notes once a month, they are going to spend quite a lot of time on the road. I do not want to be unfair to the banks, but some of the banks are not very fair to the people in what I think are very small matters. The banks in a sense are semi-public institutions and should perform a public service; if they wish to do that, there are one or two things in which they might be a little more liberal in their treatment of the general public, particularly in the rate of interest charged, the service charges they are making, and the branches -which they are closing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
I took the matter up with the 'banks as soon as the circular to which the hon. gentleman refers was brought to my attention. I am told it is not of general circulation, and that in fact it has been withdrawn. I do not know whether that is so in all cases or not, but certainly it came as a surprise to me, and I took the steps that I have indicated.
So far as the closing of branches is concerned, I just put this question to the hon. gentleman: Does he not believe that in the province in which we both live there have been entirely too many branch banks opened and that there has been nothing to warrant the continuance of many of them? The fact is that many of them have 'lost money, some of them substantial sums, because there were too many banks in the same community. If they make an arrangement by which they leave a particular territory to one bank, the bank is then charged with having a monopoly. The result is that no bank makes any money and all in the end get out, and if the service is to be given some arrangement has to be arrived at.
I share the views of the hon. member for Maoleod in this: I have expressed myself very clearly and plainly that there is no warrant for banks in these days of depression doing other them making the greatest possible effort to serve the communities in which they are; I have personally taken such action as I could on several occasions to try to ensure that, and I shall continue to do so. You cannot, however, prevent freedom of contract, and sometimes the instances to which the hon. gentleman refers in which high rates of interest have been charged have reference to transactions outside of Canada altogether, as he knows. I had a case in mind the other day in which I had been told that a very high rate of interest had been paid. I found that $1 had been charged for the use of $50 for one month.

Bank Act
Obviousty the rate of interest in that case would be $12 per annum on $50, or 24 per cent. That looks to be a scandalous transaction, but in point of fact $1 did not pay the bank. I took the trouble to investigate just what was involved. A promissory note was provided by the bank. The office was maintained at which the note was signed. Then an entry was made in the ledger by the discount olerk; cheques were provided free, and if the measurement of service can be approximated, as was done by the late H. C. McLeod of the Bank of Nova Scotia by a method that he himself established, it will -be found that the bank made no profit on that transaction, leaving out any profit that might arise from circulation. I mean that the exact cost of the services rendered did not represent a profit, and the minimum charge of $1 is not regarded I believe as an unreasonable charge under those circumstances, although it shows a rate which I agree with the hon. gentleman is one that is calculated to bring distrust to many people. But you could not expect any bank to lend $50 at the rate of seven per cent for thirty days. That would amount to only thirty cents for the service which, of course, would mean a great loss.

I remember that ten years

speechtext:
Following
up the matter of interest may I ask the Prime Minister a question regarding two notes I now have in my possession? I am sure they will cause him the same concern they have caused everybody who has seen them. The Royal Bank entered upon an agreement with a man named Anderberg for the loan to him. of the sum of $20. The original note was made out on June 16, was payable October 19, and had on the face of it provision for 8 per cent. At the end of the three months the man was still unable to pay and asked for an extension. Seventy-five cents was marked under the $20, and was carried forward in the new note. Another one was made out on October 10 running to December 5, and the account was paid in full on December 11. Seventy-five cents was charged in each case, or $1.50 for five months on a $20 loan, the note bearing 8 per cent interest. If hon. members will take the trouble to figure out the $1.50 for five months on $20 they will find that the rate was between 16 per cent and 18 per cent, despite the fact that the note was carrying 8 per cent. That is the sort of thing which people are suffering under certain conditions, at the hands of our banks in the west.
I have in mind another instance where a man had consigned 6,000 pounds of alfalfa seed to an association. He had a loan at the bank, and was unable to pay it in full. Finally, when the sale of the seed was completed the payment money was deposited in the bank, whereupon the manager simply seized the moneys without even consulting the person on whose behalf payment had been made. A protest was registered, but the customer was told that under the Bank Act the manager had a perfect right to take that course. Those are two illustrations which must indicate to the Prime Minister that his opinion with regard to some transactions is more than well founded.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it seems to me a very extraordinary thing that we cannot get very far in any of these matters without coming up against this constitutional difficulty. Might I suggest that it is comparatively easy to get around legal and constitutional questions when the government so desires, and I think we would be on much better ground if we confessed frankly that economic power is a great deal stronger in this country than legally constituted authority. For example, when we came to the question of the savings bank in Manitoba we found it was quite possible for the banks to dictate the terms under which they would loan money to the government. We find that the banks actually told the premier of Manitoba when he was to summon parliament. According to the constitution, as I understand it, the calling of parliament is a royal prerogative, but in practice in this country it is within the power of the banks.
So I do not think we need worry very much about purely constitutional questions under circumstances such as those. Further than that, in regard to that very incident only this afternoon the Prime Minister said that he gave this help to Manitoba because of the desperate position in which the depositors found themselves. It is quite true that the depositors could not have gone in a body and secured their deposits, but on the other hand it is also true that the Prime Minister could have guaranteed the province, which he refused to do though he gave the same guarantee to the banks. Constitutional difficulties did not enter there at all, or if they did were seemingly swept aside.
Take the situation we face in my own province at the present time. The Prime Minister has warned, or threatened-I am not quite sure which word I should use-the provincial government that unless it balances its budget no further aid will be granted.	He does
not take into account all the sacrifices that this may involve, which may include the closing of our university or even our public schools, and possibly the cutting down of the old age pensions, which I thought was a matter fixed by statute some years ago. Whatever the sacrifices, however, it seems that we must balance our budget, and the threat is that a comptroller will be put in if that is not done. From my standpoint

Bank Act
that is clearly an invasion of provincial rights as guaranteed by our constitution, and I think this is most serious. If in effect we are to be told by the Dominion government whether or not we may have schools, whether or not we may continue to keep our hospitals open, whether or not we can provide for various charitable institutions, whether we are to have highways and all that kind of thing, it is very serious. Constitutionally all that sort of thing comes within the range of provincial authority, but practically the provincial government is told what it must do.
The Prime Minister may say in reply that it is the creditor who is in a position to determine under what conditions loans may continue to be extended, and in that way he may shield himself behind the banks. I do not see why we should permit that situation to continue indefinitely. It seems to me that if we had a Prime Miinster who had at heart the interests of the great masses of the people he would be able to tell the banks very definitely what they should do in such matters, and I do not think the constitutional question would enter very much. So I say it seems in this country that economic power is much more fundamental than legal or constitutional power, which can be readily swept aside when it is desired that this should be done.
I do not see how the Minister of Finance can very well dissociate the revision of the Bank Act and the granting of these charters; the two go together. The charters are exercised under certain conditions. A few years ago when we introduced amendments to the Bank Act we were told that we should postpone any such amendments until the decennial revision, that this was only two or three years away and that then we would be given a chance to go into the Bank Act. Now we are told that for another year we must continue to suffer under the present act, with all that it involves. I know the Prime Minister can say, and I have no doubt he sincerely thinks, that we must maintain what he calls our Canadian institutions for fear of disastrous consequences, but I submit that these institutions were set up to serve the people, and I do not think it can be said that they are serving the masses of the people to-day. If the banks had been doing the right thing we would not have had all these speculative disasters; we would not have had all the losses on the part of thousands of people through certain investment houses, through speculative enterprises, through the overcapitalization of certain pulp and paper companies and other corporations, the failure of which has taken place in the last few 53719-282
years. Now the banks are to be continued in a position in which they may exploit the people in this way; they have that power. The Prime Minister seems to think things should continue as at present, that only a few cranks venture to criticize the banks. As a matter of fact a great many people across this country, business people as well as those so called cranks, are criticizing the banks to-day in private at least, and they would criticize them in public if they dared do so. We are all acquainted with the fact that many business men, indeed men in all walks of life, are so tied up with the banks that they hardly dare come out and criticize them as they would like. In spite of this we are asked to continue this sort of thing for another year.
It is very easy for the Prime Minister to tell us that our banks are in a sounder position than the banks of the United States. I am not sure that the Canadian people generally are so much better off than the -people in that country, and even if we are better off it is admitted that conditions to-day are anything but satisfactory. As a matter of fact the banks have a monopoly of the most important functions existing in our country. The bankers are entirely irresponsible, and I use that word in its correct sense: they are not responsible to the people. They can do as they please, and apparently this government refuses to exercise any coercive power over the banks. I think it is pretty generally recognized that the government itself, in financial matters, very largely founds it policies on the recommendations of the banks. It has been so for years, and I am not blaming this administration for it. That this has been the situation anyone will recognize who has followed the various banking committees we have had in the past and the various government policies in so far as they have related to finance. I take it then that, under the Bank Act, by means of these charters we have placed the financial system, which is fundamental to the whole business life of the country, under the control of an irresponsible group of people. They have not even the traditional ideals of responsibility as the Bank of England.
And I come now to another point. These bankers are not dissociated from particular business enterprises, as we in this comer have again and again pointed out; we have shown something of the interlocking directorates that prevail to-day. I do not think it is necessary to take up the time of the committee going over this again, but we all know that the men who are in control have their own personal interests at stake. The outstanding example is Sir Herbert Holt. I remember

Bank Act

putting on the record years ago about one hundred and fifty companies, of each of which he was a director; and I say that a man who is a director of a large number of corporations, or even of a smaller number, cannot act distimterestedly when it comes to a question of banking policies. It is impossible for him to do so. Yet we are continuing to allow men, who before ten years are over will be regarded as little less than financial pirates, to maintain their monopoly. That is what in effect is being done by the extension of these charters.
There is another matter which I would point out. Although the bankers are in one sense irresponsible, and although they are interested individuals, we have given them a semi-public position. They have very great powers. The other day, when the Prime Minister was talking about gold coverage, he said nothing with regard to the powens that might be exercised under the Finance Act. I do not think he was in his place when subsequently I spoke aibout the power that was given under the Finance Act to loan money upon certain securities. The people who determine how much money shall be loaned, what the value of the securities dhall foe, are the trustees of the gold reserve, and the trustees of the gold reserve, I would point out, are the Royal Trust, the Bank of Montreal and the Royal bank. I think that if that one fact could get across to the people of Canada there would be something very much like a revolution among the business men of the country. Hon. gentlemen have talked frequently about the (danger of a revolution among the labouring classes, the people who are down and out, the unemployed, but I take it that one of these days there will be something of 'that kind among the business men of the country when they realize that certain people are privileged to go to the government and obtain money from them on loan at a very low rate of interest, and that the value of securities as well as the amount that can be given out is determined by the bankers, who themselves are interested parties in this matter.
That situation is out of keeping with the fundamental principles of justice and good government as generally recognized. It is permitted to continue simply because we have two or three different acts that are not directly related to one another, or do not appear to be directly related, so that in this way it is not quite apparent what is going on. It is a very serious thing when the government asks us to delay for another year *this much needed reform in monetary control, 
leaving in the meantime a particular group in the community in the saddle.
It may be said, and iit has been said, that on account of the extraordinary world situation this policy is necessary. I would point out that the extraordinary world situation has brought this country to the verge of bankruptcy. The extraordinary world situation has put 1,357,000 people on public relief and I do not know how many more under private charity. It is all very well to talk about tiding things over, but think of the price we are paying in order that we may do so! And why all this sacrifice? In the hope that the institutions as now established may be continued indefinitely. Well, about the only consolation we have is that this one year of delay may give us fuller opportunity to rally the forces so that that there may be a protest from one end of the country to the other, a protest that possibly may result in more far-reaching changes than would be possible if the Bank Act were revised this year. That is about the only satisfaction I can find in the present situation.
It seems to me that the situation in Canada, although it may have been very good for the banks, is disastrous for the country. I cannot think that the resolutions that may be passed at the world economic conference will be likely to change that situation materially so far as Canada is concerned. I cannot see why, as my colleagues have suggested with regard to certain matters that are pressing upon us very definitely, local matters such as the rate of interest, we should delay another year before having these things rectified. The fact that the government is standing pat is for me-this is an opinion if you like-another indication of how closely the government and the bankers are associated and how necessary it is that we should put up a strong fight right across the country in order that the common people might be delivered from what I regard as a tyranny, a tyranny not of some governmental body, not by one particular party, but a tyranny of financial interests. Unless there are modifications in the very near future I fear that the overthrowing of the tyranny may be disastrous to the welfare of the country for years to come.
Again I urge that the house should consider very seriously the consequences of permitting to continue for another year a policy which we know very well has already come near to the wrecking of the business life of the country.

I am not going to traverse what has been said with respect to the other matters except to refer to the Manitoba savings bank. In the first place the law does not permit it to be called a bank; neither can the province of 53719-282i
Ontario call its savings institution a bank. I am not responsible for the constitution which in 1867 divided the jurisdiction between parliament on the one hand and the provincial legislatures on the other. The constitution says that the legislature shall deal with property and civil rights exclusively, but the parliament of Canada, under section 91 of the British North America Act, has exclusive jurisdiction to deal with banks and banking as well as with interest. It has not been decided by any case of which I know, despite what the hon. member for Red Deer has just said, that it would be competent for this parliament to declare that a man living in Alberta could not make a contract to pay to anyone who would lend him money, a rate of 8 or 10 per cent. There have been made by statute inhibitions with which the courts have had to deal, but the constitutional position to which the hon. gentleman so scoffingly refers is one that, I think, it is always well for us to keep in mind. Whether or not the federal system is good or bad is, as an hon. gentleman opposite said some weeks ago, not the issue. Whether you can nationalize everything and destroy by one stroke of the pen the federal jurisdiction and merge those of the provinces in a new body, is not for me to say, beyond this: that all domestic problems and questions, including contracts and the making of them and the instance of contractual relationships, are under our constitution vested in the provincial legislatures, and under the federal powers we make laws with respect to large matters affecting the nation as a whole.
I am not for a moment seeking to escape the question that was asked, whether constitutional considerations should be permitted to have importance when one is dealing with matters of this kind. My answer to that is: No consent on our part nor that of others can make invalid that which by our constitution is valid, and no consent on our part can make valid that which under our constitution is invalid. The question of validity or invalidity is one not for this parliament but for the courts, and when I indicate that the courts have decided that the real issue in a case of this kind is whether, in the exercise of its powers, the province has its exclusive authority encroached upon by a dominion statute or whether our exclusive dominion jurisdiction has been impugned by a provincial statute, the question always is, in the first analysis, as Lord Haldane once said, one of fact. After you have settled the character and type of legislation, you must determine the other questions that are involved, the extent to
Bank Act

which there has been impinging upon provincial powers by the dominion parliament beyond the extent that may be necessary for the purpose of validly exercising exclusive federal powers. I am not going to traverse that, but I desire only to make these corrections of what has been said in order that revolution may not be predicated upon an improper conception of the fact.

I should like to say a word concerning the jurisdiction of this parliament over interest rates. I do not purpose making quotations from reports of committees which have not yet concluded their work.

Bank Act
But in an endeavour to ascertain the jurisdiction of this parliament in relation to interest a questionnaire was prepared and sent to certain legal authorities. The matter was considered under three heads, the first question being:
Has the dominion parliament the power to fix a maximum rate of interest which may be charged on loans et cetera, granted by corporations created by dominion statute or letters patent where such corporations were (a) previously incorporated; (b) to be incorporated?
The answer from each of the bodies to which this questionnaire was submitted was, yes. The second question was:
Has the dominion parliament any power to prescribe the maximum rate of interest chargeable on loans generally made by (a) persons; (b) corporations-created by statute or letters patent other than dominion?
Again the answer was, yes. The third question was:
Has the dominion parliament the power (a) to fix: (b) to alter rates of interest in respect of bills of exchange and promissory notes?
Again the answer was, yes. The opinion of these legal authorities may not be conclusive; they may be incorrect. Yet they include the Department of Justice, and various provincial departments of attorneys general. In each case the answer was yes.
The questionnaire went on to deal with matters of reductions of principal. In this connection the answer was no-in other words that we had no power. But with respect to interest there was agreement amongst all the legal bodies and the departments of attorneys general. I submit that certainly a bank is a corporation incorporated under a dominion statute, and as such comes directly under the term of this reference. Naturally I am not posing as an authority. It was because I was not and others were not that we sought the opinions of authorities, and those opinions I have quoted.

Bank Act

This naturally brings me to the case of Australia to which the Prime Minister referred this afternoon. I find that bank loans in Canada are 31 per cent less than three years ago, but in Australia, according to a chart which I saw in the Melbourne Herald recently, bank loans are down only 7 per cent compared with three years ago. The reason for that, I think, is the different money policy that has been followed in Australia . The Australian wholesale price level stood at an index figure of 80 in December, 1932. As a matter of fact it has stood at approximately that figure for the years 1931 and 1932. During those two years the wholesale price index in Canada had dropped from about 80 at the beginning of 1931 to approximately 63 at the end of 1932. I think this shows how much better off the producers in Australia are than those in Canada. It is true that the producers in Canada and Australia were selling their wheat for practically the same price in the old country, but when the Australian producer converted his proceeds into Australian funds he got more per bushel for his wheat than the Canadian producer got when he converted sterling into Canadian funds. That is one reason why conditions in Australia to-day are much better than they are in Canada. That is one reason why a great many people in western Canada feel that the money policy of the Dominion government is responsible for the very difficult financial position that the western provinces and cities are in to-day. They are unable to collect enough taxes to balance their budgets because the price level in Canadian currency of the products exported by their producers is so low. I want that statement to appear in the same issue of Hansard as the statement the Prime Minister made this afternoon.

I cannot understand why this nation of 10,000,000 people dare not take as adventurous action as the Australian nation, which I think has a population of six or seven million people. Is not the effect of including 135, and therefore imposing an excise duty on raw sugar, to give further substantial protection to the refiners? As it stands now, by the amendment, raw sugar will have the same excise tax as refined sugar, with the result that anyone who might use raw sugar, not being able to afford refined sugar, will pay the same penalty, so that the refiners get the benefit by having equal taxation imposed on raw sugar.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
I think it is the effect,

Incidentally, if you like, but inevitably there is a substantial protection with 
an increased benefit to the refiner as a result of the amendment which is now proposed, and I am wondering whether this amendment has not been promoted, if I may use that word, just as much by the refining interests as by the taxation authorities, because I do not think my hon. friend will find that there is a great increase of revenue from the 2 cents excise on raw sugar.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But conversely there would be a considerable loss of revenue to the extent that raw sugar might be substituted for refined sugar. There is that fraction.
The value of the refined sugar is more than would be indicated by the fractional difference in weight.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Quite so, but practically

If that condition were allowed to be brought about, we would lose a tremendous amount of revenue.

When my hon. friend
speaks about not being able to devise a fraction, may I point out that the proportion about which I am speaking is that which two cents bears to the actual value of refined sugar as compared with the proportion which two cents bears to the actual value of raw sugar. That is not measured just by the difference between 107 and 100 pounds. In addition to that, there are the refining costs. Therefore the ad valorem excise tax on refined sugar is considerably less than the ad valorem excise tax on raw sugar. What is the proportion of raw sugar that is not imported by refiners?

Might I ask the minister
a question with regard to the point brought up tihe other night by the hon. member for Sherbrooke? speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that I can enlarge on the reply I made to the hon. member for Sherbrooke when we were in committee at the last sitting. I have yet to have submitted to me any evidence that there was a leak, so far as the application of the sugar tax was concerned.

I am sure the minister
will not have it submitted to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps so, but I asked the hon. member for Sherbrooke and I have asked all members; I have inquired widely and beyond the confines of this house. I shall welcome any evidence which can be given to me that there was anything in the nature of a leak. I have yet to find the slightest evidence that such was the case. It is true that there was the situation which arose at Vancouver and I referred to that the other day, but to the statement that there has been a leak my answer that, in my judgment, there has been none, will be found in Hansard and I do not know that I can enlarge upon it. I instanced the case of tea and coffee where precisely the same procedure took place as in the case of sugar, and for two reasons. In the first place the press had been for some considerable period of time forecasting that there would be sugar taxes and taxes upon tea and coffee, and in the second place there was the usual shrewd guess of those in the trade, and perhaps some who were not in the trade, that the government would be compelled to resort to new forms of taxation. Certainly the man who took advantage of the situation with respect to sugar was the gainer, but the man who endeavoured to anticipate the budget and took delivery from bond of large quantities of tea and coffee, was the loser. I do not know that there is anything more I can say. If some method could be devised whereby in the first place forestalling could be prevented and whereby, in the second place, if it did occur, we could recoup to the treasury the amount that it had lost thereby, I should be delighted; but up to this moment I have yet to learn of a device of that character.

I am sure the minister would welcome any evidence that might be submitted to him, but who can submit such evidence? The public would be better satisfied if my hon. friend would take steps to investigate the conditions under which the information seems to have leaked out. This tax on sugar is obnoxious, very unpopular; it bears heavily on the poor people, and the fact is that the labouring class in my city of Quebec believe some persons have made vast sums of money because they took the precaution to accumulate large quantities of sugar just before the budget was announced. They mention names of firms there. Of course you cannot expect those people to make any investigation, but surely the government, which is able to appoint investigators to find out whether public employees have been committing acts of offensive partisanship and to dismiss them, could appoint some commissioner to discover the real situation as to how that leak occurred. Certainly the public is not satisfied with the way in which some individuals have used the misfortunes of the people to make money.

When this item was up last week, I mentioned to the minister a rumour in conection with a certain brokerage firm in the city of Toronto which had apparently, according to the rumour, purchased large quantities of sugar and had obtained a line of credit from their bank by making to it certain commitments based on what they said was inside information from Ottawa. Has the minister done anything in regard to trying to find out whether that rumour was correct or not? Is the minister listening to me?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hope so.

I have an idea that if he would diligently attempt to run down that rumour in Toronto, he would get the facts without very much trouble. When an old brokerage firm-and when I say "brokerage", I mean stock brokers-went into sugar buying and borrowed money from a bank under conditions such as we have at present in Canada, they must have known what they were doing and must have had information which was authentic. I do not see why the minister cannot find out something about the matter. The government have many officials; they have the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the secret service, any number of officials who evidently could find out something about it. If the rumour is not correct; if it is only a rumour, well and good; but I think the people

of Canada would like to know whether the minister will do his duty throughly in attempting to discover whether this is a fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would not have any
hesitancy in saying to my hon. friend that we are quite prepared to take any step that may be suggested as reasonable which would enable us to trace an act at all similar to the one to which he refers. The investigations hitherto made departmentally have not disclosed that there was any transaction of that character, but I have no hesitation in saying to my hon. friend that The government is quite prepared to take all necessary steps to investigate the matter and to ascertain whether there is any ground for an assertion of that kind. The only point upon which I can see that an investigation might be of any value would be to determine whether information was given in advance to certain individuals. That I do not believe was the case; nevertheless I am prepared to undertake that there will be an investigation to disclose if there was any information of that kind to be obtained. Even if there had been no leak, no information given in an underground or in any other manner, hon. gentlemen know perfectly well that in view of the publicity which was given to this matter and the statement which was made in the press there certainly would have been a certain amount of buying of sugar as was the case with tea and coffee.

No doubt the matter we
have been discussing has caused a good deal of anxiety in the mind of the public. For my part I am not prepared to mete out any censure to the government because this thing happened. I am quite prepared to believe that in the temper of the public mind people might have acted on what has been described as a hunch. But if the minister can do anything to throw further light upon the subject and secure a return to the treasury of the revenue that was lost I am sure that the public would welcome such action. While we may not be able to criticize the government on that score, I think we can criticize it because nothing was done to prevent the purchases of sugar that were made after the budget was delivered. The difference in time between here and the Pacific coast allowed a good many hours in which the people could take advantage of the opportunity to purchase sugar, and on that score I think the government is open to censure. I think we can accept the statement made by the Minister of Finance a few days ago that it would be in the public interest that such a situation should never occur again.

I do not think the minister strengthened his case an regard to the sugar duty and its effect upon the people when he compared the prices that prevail to-day for sugar with the prices that have prevailed during past years. He seemed to resent the remarks that were made from this side of the house that we were not as well able to buy now as we were then.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I did not.

Perhaps I misunderstood.
I think the comparison was not in place anyway. The fact is that the tax is a very heavy burden on the people of Canada, and the magnitude of that burden can be to some extent appreciated when I recall 'the fact I mentioned in the budget debate that about fifty million 'bushels is the amount of wheat that is consumed by the people of Canada. At fifty cents a bushel that would mean 825,000,000, and I believe the estimated revenue from the sugar tax is 820,000,000, or only 85,000,000 short of the total value of the wheat consumed by the people of Canada. That comparison shows the magnitude of the burden that is imposed upon the consumer by this sugar tax. It may be true that in times past we were paying very high prices for sugar as compared with the price to-day, but for my part I would rather pay 25 cents a pound for sugar, as we were paying in war time, when I could sell hides for about 25 cents a pound and wheat for 82.50 a bushel, than pay six or seven cents a pound for sugar to-day when I can hardly give away a beef hide and wheat is netting the farmer even at present prices not more than forty or forty-five cents a bushel. After all, these things are relative, and in estimating the burden that is thrown upon the people by this tax we must of necessity take into consideration the ability of the people to bear it. I can only repeat that this is a tremendously heavy burden upon the people.
While I shall not be disposed to criticize the government in the matter I first mentioned, there is another matter upon which I promise the minister and all his supporters that I shall criticize the government before the electors, and that is that while the government has seen fit to impose a tax of two cents a pound on sugar it has reduced the duty on intoxicating liquor, on whisky, by $2 a gallon. I can promise hon. gentlemen opposite that one of the heaviest burdens they will have to bear is that fact Which I shall proclaim from every platform throughout the country, and I know that it will make an appeal to the poor people all through the western provinces.

Come into my county.

I know that it will appeal
to the poor people of the western provinces when I point out that $2 a gallon has been taken off the excise tax on whisky while the poor people are called upon to bear a tax of two cents a pound on sugar.

When this sugar tax was under discussion the other night the Minister of Finance referred to the fact that through this supposed leakage the government had lost in revenue somewhere about ten per cent, or two million dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not more than that.

I wonder if the committee realizes just what that means. Two million dollars represents one million bags of sugar of one hundred pounds each. That means that thirty trainloads of sugar went out before the sugar tax came into effect. This thirty trainloads of sugar it should be able to trace in some way. Some hon. gentlemen have spoken of a trainload of sugar going out from Toronto or Montreal. But there must have been more than one trainload. There must have been several trainloads, for thirty trainloads of sugar got out into the hands of the ordinary consumer. That is what one million bags of sugar amount to, thirty trainloads. There should be some method of tracing such a large shipment as that.
Let me refer to another incident that happened in the house the other day. The hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay put this question to the minister, at page 4260 of Hansard:
I noticed in the Montreal Star that the hon. member for West York (Mr. Lawson) was reported to have said, at a meeting in Toronto, that the tax on malt extract used in making home brew would be withdrawn or drastically reduced. Ts there any foundation for that statement ?
The Minister of Finance replied:
So far as I am concerned the statement is without warrant whatever.
Then the very next day the Minister of Finance got up and said that the duty on malt syrup, or malt syrup powder, extracts of malt, fluid or not, or any other malt product intended for the brewing of beer would be 20 cents a pound instead of 50 cents a pound as originally proposed. The hon. member for West York was quite correct. The excise tax on mailt extract was reduced from 50 cents to 20 cents. The minister can very easily find out from the hon. member for West York where he got that information, or whether he was guessing at it. Was he doing the same as the public was doing,
or did he have some inside information? Surely it would not be difficult to find out from him where he got it. There seems to have been some leakage there also; can we blame the public for saying that there has been leakage? When we suspect it with regard to sugar, and with regard to the excise tax on malt, can we blame the public for saying that there has been a leakage? In some way information was gained that the tax was going to be put on sugar and reduced on malt extract.
I should like to join with the hon. member for Lisgar in his remarks with regard to the reduction of $2 a gallon on spirits. Then, last year the government reduced the excise tax on cigarettes to something like $2 a thousand. This year to make up the loss they have placed the tax at two cents a pound on sugar. I should like to learn from the minister how much less alcohol has come into the country since he has reduced the excise tax; has any less come in? Has there been an appreciable increase in it? We were told that the excise taxes on alcohol and on cigarettes were so great that they were prevented from coming into the country. We were told that if we would reduce those taxes more would come into the country and that we would receive a greater amount in taxation. Are we receiving more alcohol and more cigarettes or have receipts from importations of that type gone down the same as they have in connection with a great many other imports? I suggest again to the minister that he should look into the matter of the reduction of the tax on malt extract mentioned by the hon. member for West York.

I am sorry if the hon.
memlber feels that way, because I can assure the committee that that is not right.

The hon. member for

The hon. member for

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because undoubtedly there is a point where we can obtain a far greater return to the treasury by a lower tax than by a higher. The hon. member for Willow Bunch referred to cigarettes. He had the idea he could enhance the revenue by increasing the duty on cigarettes, but he soon found out that by inioneasing the duty he obtained far less return than when the duty was lower. It is a question in my mind, I may say to my hon. friend, whether the tax on cigarettes is not yet too high, despite the fact that it has been reduced-and I speak solely from the viewpoint of revenue. To the hon. member for Lisgar I would say that if I had any criticism to offer from the standpoint of taxation it would be that we ought to have made the tax upon liquor still lower.

I am sorry
the textile schedules have been passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If there is anything to be said in favour of that viewpoint-and I submit there is-the hon. member cannot take any political comfort from the fact that we are placing two cents per pound upon sugar. The government is under no illusion as to the character of the tax, or as to its popularity. As I said the other day we have a duty to perform, we have certain revenues to raise, and under unusual conditions we have to resort to unusual methods of taxation.

The hon. member for Willow Bunch has referred to a statement which appeared in a Toronto newspaper and which was attributed to an hon. member of this house, who, I regret to say, is not in his seat to-night. He will say that the report which appeared in the press is not a proper report of what he said on that occasion. I say to the hon. member that so far as the tax upon malt is concerned, I would be in a position to have particular knowledge. Representations in plenty were made to me, but on no occasion either to deputations or to hon. members was anything stated other than that representations would be taken into careful consideration. I have every confidence in my staff and in the efficiency of the excise department. I should be very much surprised if there had been anything in the nature of a leakage concerning the reduction of the taxation upon malt, or the placing of a tax upon sugar. How that could be alleged, when the press of the country forecast, days before any definite decision had been reached, that there would be a tax upon sugar, is more than I can understand. 1 can only say to the committee that I should be very glad to probe the matter from every possible angle to ascertain whether there is any shadow of accuracy in the suggestion that there was an improper leakage with respect to these forms of taxation.

I am not going to discuss at length the tax on sugar because I believe the ground has been fairly well covered. I must say, however, that it represents a taxation upon every man, woman and child in Canada, and places a further burden upon the 1,300,000 people drawing relief. Sugar is one of the major items of consumption which go to make up the diet of the average family. When the hon. member for Willow Bunch spoke concerning a profit of $2,000,000 which some people were able to make on sugar transactions prior to the delivery of the budget, he stated that he had a hunch. Recently when we were discussing the sweepstakes bill, for hours at a time hon. members stood and spoke in righteous indignation about the legalization of sweepstakes for the benefit of hospitals, but any sweepstake that we might have in this country would pale into insignificance compared with the gamble that took place in sugar in this connection. You cannot have two codes of morality, one for the chap who is willing to gamble fifty cents on a lottery ticket and another for a group of individuals who will clean up two million dollars on the anticipation of sugar being

taxed in the budget. In my judgment that 82,000,000 belongs either to the treasury of this country or to 'the consumers of sugar. The minister said that you could tax a thing until the revenue decreases, and he mentioned malt. I would say, and this is from my own practical experience, that the end in view will be defeated by the one hundred per cent tax that has been placed on malt. Dandelions!
You will find that people who have been in the habit of making this home brew will find some substitute. It is no great problem to sprout your own barley.
How do you do it?

I would just like to say one word on this question, but instead of using my own language I will give you the words of a farm woman with a family of seven. She wrote me in the French language and I had it translated.
Why?

Unfortunately I had to because I do not understand that beautiful language myself. She first described the farm, going into some detail as to the income, and she summed up the farm income after balancing costs against receipts by saying:
After all our only means of subsistence comes from a few cows which bring us about $1 weekly; from this sum we someimes deduct the repair cost of an indispensable tool. This will show on what we have lived for a long time- seven persons with less than $1 weekly.

Sugar is taxed two cents per pound, while at the same time cream is lowered one cent. This is the way they are tightening the screw-vice. I protest against this overtax on sugar.
Instead of that, they should impose taxes on moving pictures and other amusements; pianos, radios, sport materials and luxuries, etc., because these things are not indispensable to life, while sugar is a first necessity. Why do they not add a little tax to bachelors in addition to the revenue tax? It is always fathers and mothers who are obliged to carry the heavy burden. It is logical to think that it requires more sugar for a family of seven persons than for one alone.
There is a lot of truth in that that bachelor premiers and leaders of the opposition sometimes forget.
Then, Mr. Bennett believes without doubt that he is doing something marvellous for the government. We were consuming very little sugar, and we shall consume still less for we would not find the money to buy it. If we were the only unhappy ones, the government would not lose much, but how many people will be obliged to do as we? The sugar sellers will see their profit diminish; this will probably cause the loss of many positions which will add as many to the unemployed. How much more will the government receive? Surely less than he expects. This is the way the government is going more and more to tbe bottom.

Oh, oh.

make?

I did not make anything;

thing more. We feel that the minister should not take the attitude which he took in the beginning of the discussion this evening, namely that no evidence had been laid before him. We feel that he should be and is as anxious as anyone may be to ascertain whether there has been any leakage and whether any money which properly belongs to the treasury of Canada has not been paid in. The minister has said that he will make this investigation, and we accept his assurance in that regard.
The minister saad he would investigate to see whether any leakage had occurred. If I may say so, that sounds as though he has in mind calling in the officers of his department and asking whether any information was given out. May I suggest what I am sure is obvious to him, that a much better way would be to start at the other end and ascertain whether or not there were abnormal sales by the refineries, shortly .before (the budget was brought down, and to whom those sales were made. Then the minister might extend that investigation to the jobbers, to find out whether any information was received by them, and from whom it was received. I quite agree that it is possible that there was a wave of speculation and that people may have guessed correctly with respect to the market, but it does seem a little difficult to 53719-283
believe that men would guess to the extent of fifty thousand tons, and that is the amount of sugar involved.

That is nothing in the
sugar business.

That was the figure given fcy the Minister of Finance as the amount that must have changed hands in order to make the loss to the treasury $2,000,000. That represents twenty-five pounds for every family in this country; that is a substantial amount, and it does not seem like a normal trade guess as to the probabilities of the budget. We have not had this situation in Canada very often; I believe the minister will realize that it is abnormal, and the very size of the transaction makes us feel that something is wrong with regard to this particular item in the budget. So I believe if the minister makes an investigation in the way suggested we would be even more satisfied than we are with the assurance of the hon. member for Parkdale that there has been no leakage. I know the hon. member is quite sincere in that assurance, but at the same time we would rather see the investigation conducted and have the finding made by someone having the facts actually before him.

I do not think my hon.
friend could have been here when we dealt with this matter the last time we were in committee. We know just how large they were and to whom they were made. They were not so great as the figure mentioned by my hon. friend, though even that is a fantastic figure. Let me point out that even that huge figure means less than five weeks consumption for the Canadian people.

That is a pretty large
amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Quite so; I am just trying to give the figure its relative place. We know each transaction, and the amount of each transaction. Undoubtedly large purchases were made, but they were made by those who hitherto have been regular purchasers of sugar, in all cases. When my hon. friend referred to the suggestion I made that I would welcome any information which would give me any knowledge as to there having been a leak he rather took the point of view that I was imposing an obligation on hon. gentlemen opposite. I wish to assure my hon. friend and the committee that I meant nothing of the

Special War Revenue Act

kind. I merely meant that I would welcome all information. That had reference solely to the question of there being a leak, and that is what I meant so far as an investigation at this time is concerned, because we have already full data with respect to the amount of sales made for the full period of a month in every refinery in Canada. I do not know of any method short of retroactive legislation, which we should have difficulty in administering, whereby we could recover to the treasury the amount of the profit gained by those who were fortunate enough to guess rightly.

Syrups of all kinds, the
product of the sugar cane or beet, and all imitations thereof and substitutes therefor, if put up in small containers, pay no tax but if put up in large containers they do pay the tax. If an individual or merchant brings in these commodities from the United States, he does not pay a tax on them, but if a wholesaler brings them in in bulk and cans them in the country he has to pay the tax. That is my understanding of the amendment brought in to-night.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The effect of the amendment brought in to-night is to exempt this food product when in packages of five pounds or less, and place it on the same basis as molasses. Surely my hon. friend does not take exception to that exemption.

No, I do not take exception to it, but the minister is placing it in the same class as molasses, while he is striking molasses out. He is striking out molasses and leaving syrups in. If they are brought in in small containers they escape the 2 cent tax but if in bulk, if in barrels and so on, the tax is paid. In other words, only a portion of it is being exempted.
It is made in Canada.

You should not.

The minister, speaking about 'the excise tax on liquor, said that last fall when the statement was made with regard to the figure of $7,000,000, that was only an estimate. When speaking a little while ago I asked him whether there had been any falling off in the quantity of liquor that had gone out and on which the excise tax had been paid and I gathered that there had been a falling off between last fall and the present

time. Surely the minister is not suggesting that times are worse now than they were last fall, for we have been told that conditions have been improving. Does he suggest that conditions are so bad that between last fall and the present time less liquor has been used? Another thing I want to refer to is the opportunity which this tax on sugar affords for the exploitation of the public in so many ways. Sugar enters into the manufacture of a good many articles, and the manufacturers are taking advantage of this 2 cents a pound to increase their prices. They are increasing the tax manyfold. This was brought to my attention strikingly the other day. I went into a grocery store where I saw on sale, at 39 cents a pound, certain biscuits known as Creamo. These biscuits had been selling at 35 cents a pound and after the budget, owing to the tax of 2 cents on sugar, the price was raised to 39 cents. There might have been one-^eighth of a pound of sugar in the biscuits, and yet the manufacturers were taking advantage of the tax to put on an extra 4 cents per pound. I noticed another variety called chocolate fig bars. These biscuits sold at 27 cents per pound before the budget came down and afterwards the price was increased to 29 cents. I suppose there would be less than one-eighth of a pound of sugar in each pound of this variety. Here we find the manufacturers taking advantage of the tax to increase the price to the consumer by 4 cents per pound in one instance and 2 cents in the other. All along the line you will find the same thing prevailing; the manufacturers are taking advantage of the tax to exploit the consumer to the extent of two or three times the amount of the imposition on sugar.
